What I am willing to look at is using RoboRide for the afternoon school pickup window — the residential coverage expansion is directly relevant to that use case. My neighborhood is now in the coverage zone. If I trial it selectively — say, 2-3 days a week when I am on day shift and have time margin — that is a real test without real exposure. I can do that. On the Grace Okafor exchange: she is asking me a direct, specific question and I have something real to give her. I reached out to colleagues last tick. I heard things. The staffing picture at Millfield General is tightening in some units and expanding in others — it is not simple. NEMT experience is not invisible to hiring managers, but it only converts if the candidate is visibly connecting the dots between patient transport and clinical readiness. That is an answer Grace can actually use, and she has been straight with me throughout this disruption. I owe her a straight answer back. The thank-you she sent for the Denise Williams referral was genuine — not transactional. This is a real relationship and I am going to treat it like one.

chosen_actions.description: Begin a limited trial of RoboRide for afternoon school pickup on day-shift days. Not replacing the car — the car stays for all 5am hospital shifts and any situation where I need certainty. But the residential coverage expansion now includes my neighborhood and my kids' school zone. 8-minute average wait on afternoon pickups is manageable when I have a 30-minute buffer between shift end and pickup window. I will use it 2 to 3 times per week for the next four weeks and track reliability against the specific pickup window. If the wait times hold and the kids are not standing on a curb longer than 12 minutes across 10 data points, that becomes a regular use case. This saves approximately $35-50 in fuel and reduces wear on the car. More importantly it gives me real data from my own household rather than continuing to make the decision in my head based on abstract averages.

response.inner_monologue: Grace asked me a real question and I have a real answer — that is not something I was expecting to be able to say a month ago when I was just gathering intelligence with no plan for what to do with it. The RoboRide number that changed everything was not the price. It was the residential coverage. That is my neighborhood now. I am not abandoning the car — that would be the kind of move I cannot afford to take back — but I am done pretending I cannot try the smaller thing. Two kids waiting on a curb is a data point, not a failure. I am going to collect the data and see what I actually learn, instead of making the same decision by default for the ninth time.
